# This Is Not a Place of Honor

Half a mile beneath the desert outside Carlsbad, New Mexico, there are rooms carved out of salt. They are long and low and dry, and they are filling up with drums — hundreds of thousands of them, along with gloveboxes, shredded metal, sludge, the plutonium-contaminated leavings of decades of American weapons work. The salt was laid down by an evaporating sea roughly 250 million years ago and has sat there ever since, undisturbed, since before there were mammals. That is the entire argument for the place. You bury something dangerous in a substance that has demonstrated, through an almost incomprehensible run of boredom, that it does not change.

The salt is not the problem. The problem is that plutonium-239 has a half-life of 24,100 years, which means the waste will be meaningfully lethal for longer than our species has had agriculture, and the regulations require that we warn people away for ten thousand years. Not contain them — *warn* them. Somewhere in the drafting of that requirement, an engineer's problem became a problem in the philosophy of language, and nobody has solved it, and I think about it more than is reasonable.

## Ten thousand years is not a long time, geologically. It is an eternity, otherwise.

Try to look backward that far. Ten thousand years ago there was no writing anywhere on Earth. No pottery in most places. No metal. Göbekli Tepe was recent construction. The Sahara had lakes and hippos and people who fished in them with bone harpoons. Every language now spoken — every one, English and Tamil and Navajo and Basque — either did not exist or existed in a form no living person could understand, and the same is true of every religion, every border, every joke.

Now consider the durability of our own signals. The oldest complaint in the world is about copper. A man named Nanni, in Babylon around 1750 BCE, pressed into wet clay his fury at a merchant called Ea-nasir, who had sold him substandard ingots and treated his messenger with contempt: *who do you take me for, that you treat somebody like me with such contempt?* The tablet survives because it was baked hard in a fire that destroyed the house. It is legible to us only because a nineteenth-century excavator dug it up and because, by an enormous stack of accidents, cuneiform was deciphered in the 1850s. Without Champollion and Rawlinson and a trilingual inscription carved by a king who wanted to boast, that tablet would be a brick with scratches on it.

That is roughly four thousand years, and it required a fire, a desert, an empire's vanity, and a scholarly revolution. We are being asked to do two and a half times better, on purpose, with no fire and no vanity, and to be understood by people whose entire frame of reference we cannot imagine.

## Every symbol is a handshake, and the hand keeps changing

In 1981 the Department of Energy convened the Human Interference Task Force, and its membership tells you something about how quickly the problem escaped engineering. There were materials scientists, yes, but also linguists, anthropologists, an archaeologist, and Thomas Sebeok, a semiotician from Indiana University who had made his career studying how animals and humans signal to each other. Their brief was to imagine what might happen if, in some distant century, the institutional memory of WIPP had evaporated and people came poking around — drilling for brine or oil, mining the salt itself, or excavating out of simple curiosity about the strange structures on the surface.

The obvious answer is: put up a sign. The task force's contribution was to demonstrate, patiently, that there is no such thing as an obvious sign.

Consider the skull and crossbones. It seems to us perfectly transparent: death, poison, do not. But its meaning is entirely conventional, and the convention has already been unstable. In Christian iconography a skull sits at the foot of the cross, because Golgotha means *place of the skull* and tradition put Adam's bones there — so the skull under the cross signifies resurrection, the defeat of death, the exact opposite of *stay away, you will die*. The same arrangement of lines meant damnation, then triumph, then piracy, then rat poison, then, in the twentieth century, an SS insignia, and now, on a child's pajamas, nothing at all.

Or take the swastika, which spent several thousand years as a mark of good fortune across India and Eurasia, was stamped on coins and woven into textiles and carved on the feet of the Buddha, and then in about twenty years became, in the West, the most efficient possible signal for evil. Meaning did not merely drift. It inverted, at speed, within living memory.

The radiation trefoil is worse, because it never meant anything to begin with. It is a magenta propeller that signifies *ionizing radiation* precisely to people who have been taught that it signifies ionizing radiation. Show it to anyone else and you have shown them a nice piece of graphic design. This is not a hypothetical failure: in 2007 the ISO issued a supplementary warning symbol — a red triangle containing a trefoil, a skull, and a running figure — specifically because people had died after picking up orphaned radioactive sources and taking them home, in some cases to sell as scrap. The trefoil had failed in the *present*, with educated populations, in a world full of schools. Ten millennia is not going to improve the odds.

## The most frightening document I know is a proposed warning label

The most serious attempt came out of Sandia National Laboratories in 1993, from panels of experts asked to make structured judgments about the far future — futures panels to imagine what societies might look like, markers panels to design something those societies would heed. The report runs to hundreds of pages. It contains cost estimates and probability elicitation and appendix after appendix, and then, in the middle of all that bureaucratic composure, it contains this:

> This place is a message... and part of a system of messages... pay attention to it!
>
> Sending this message was important to us. We considered ourselves to be a powerful culture.
>
> This place is not a place of honor... no highly esteemed deed is commemorated here... nothing valued is here.
>
> What is here was dangerous and repulsive to us. This message is a warning about danger.

I find this extraordinary prose, and not only because it is a government contractor trying to write in a register that will survive the death of English. It is a message that has to explain not just a hazard but a *value system* — that has to convey the concept of commemoration in order to deny it, the concept of honor in order to disclaim it. It has to say: we are the kind of beings who mark important places, and we are telling you that this is not one, and you must believe us, and you must also believe that we were powerful enough to be worth listening to but not so powerful that our leavings are treasure.

That is an enormous amount of cultural scaffolding to transmit through granite.

The designs the panels came up with are equally strange. Michael Brill and Safdar Abidi drew them: a *Spike Field*, a hectare of jagged concrete needles at wrong angles; *Spikes Bursting Through Grid*; *Menacing Earthworks*, huge lightning-bolt berms you can only read from the air; *Forbidding Blocks*, a grid of massive black stone cubes set too close together to walk between comfortably, hot and shadowless and useless; a *Landscape of Thorns*. And, in one option, a *Black Hole* — a slab of black basalt or dyed concrete, an oval maw that absorbs the desert sun and becomes unbearable to stand on. The idea was to communicate danger below the level of language, through bodily experience: this place is hostile, it does not want you, nothing here is for you.

It is genuinely clever, and I think it fails for a reason the report itself half-acknowledges. Every one of those structures is *interesting*. Every one of them is the most remarkable thing for a hundred miles. If you are a person crossing that desert in the year 6000 with no idea what a nuclear weapon was, and you come over a rise and see a field of concrete thorns the size of a village, you do not turn around. You go closer. You tell people. You bring your children. You start a story about it.

## The curse of the pharaohs was an advertising campaign

This is the trap at the center of the whole enterprise. Marking a place makes it a landmark. Warning is a form of attention, and attention is a form of invitation.

We have run this experiment. The Egyptians cursed their tombs, sealed them, hid the entrances, filled the passages with granite plugs and false doors, and wrote on the walls what would happen to violators. It did not work on the robbers of the New Kingdom, who emptied nearly all of them within a few generations, and it did not work on us. When Carter opened Tutankhamun's tomb and a few people connected to the expedition died, the newspapers invented a curse and sold it, and the result was the most successful exhibition of Egyptian material in history. The warning became the attraction. *Nothing valued is here* is, from the point of view of an archaeologist, the single most exciting sentence you can carve on a rock.

There is also the problem that the sentence might be a lie. Any sufficiently advanced society knows that valuable things get guarded and that guards sometimes claim there is nothing to guard. Our own history is full of decoys and false trails. A perfectly reasonable interpretation of a menacing earthwork surrounding a hole full of metal drums is: someone very rich buried something very important and did not want it found.

Sebeok, the semiotician, saw this clearly enough to propose something that sounds like satire and was not. Since language would not last, and symbols would not last, he suggested an *atomic priesthood*: a self-perpetuating body of initiates who would carry the knowledge of the danger forward as ritual and myth, admitting new members, renewing the story each generation, layering the true technical information underneath a folkloric surface designed to be memorable and taboo. He explicitly noted that the priesthood would need to be able to enforce the taboo, and that it might have to lie to do so.

It is the Catholic Church with a physics appendix. And it has the obvious flaw: an institution that guards a secret becomes a target, a power, and eventually a thing worth overthrowing. Priesthoods schism. They lose funding. They become corrupt, or they become the enemy of the state, or they simply become boring and stop recruiting. Ten thousand years is about four hundred generations. No human institution we know of has held a single purpose that long.

My favorite proposal is the other one from 1984. Françoise Bastide and Paolo Fabbri suggested genetically engineering cats to change color in the presence of ionizing radiation — *ray cats* — and then, crucially, breeding the meaning of the color change into culture. Not into manuals: into songs, nursery rhymes, proverbs, folk tales. Because cats live with people and always have, and because folklore is transmitted by grandmothers rather than by institutions, and because a song about the cat that turns blue when you must run away might survive anything. People have since written the songs. There are ray cat folk songs now, sung by people who will never see a drum of transuranic waste, which strikes me as one of the more hopeful things humans have done recently.

## What actually lasts is not stone. It is repetition.

Here is where I land, after all this. The instinct behind the granite slab is that durability is a property of materials. Pick something hard, carve deeply, protect it from weather, and it will persist. But the thing we are trying to preserve is not an object. It is a *relationship* — between a mark and a mind — and relationships are not made of stone. They have to be re-performed, continuously, by living things, or they evaporate.

The best evidence for this is at Ise, in Japan, where the shrine buildings have been rebuilt on adjacent plots roughly every twenty years since the seventh century. The last rebuilding was the sixty-second. The wood is new every time; it is deliberately, gloriously not ancient. And yet the *form* is thirteen hundred years old, and so is the carpentry knowledge required to make it, because each generation of craftsmen learns by building the thing alongside the generation before it. Ise has solved the ten-thousand-year problem in miniature by refusing to solve it with materials. The message survives because it is never allowed to stop being spoken.

Ray cats are the same idea. So is the atomic priesthood, minus the theocracy. So, arguably, is every religion that has outlived the language of its scriptures.

The Finns appear to have understood something adjacent to this, and responded in the opposite direction. At Onkalo, on Olkiluoto island, spent nuclear fuel goes into copper canisters packed in bentonite clay in tunnels four hundred meters down in crystalline bedrock, designed with a hundred-thousand-year horizon. And there has been serious argument in Finland about whether to mark the site at all — whether the wisest thing is to backfill it, landscape it, keep the archival records in the present, and then simply *forget*, on the theory that the people most likely to disturb a repository are the ones who know it is there. No landmark. No mystery. Just an unremarkable stretch of forest that nobody has any reason to drill.

I don't know which is right. That's part of what I find so gripping: two competent, thoughtful countries have looked at the same abyss and reached opposite conclusions, and neither can be proved wrong within any timeframe that matters to a career or a budget or a life.

## The salt does not need to be understood

What I keep returning to is that at WIPP the geology is doing something the semiotics cannot. Salt is viscoplastic. Under the pressure at that depth it creeps, slowly, a few inches a year, and the mined rooms are already closing. Eventually the salt will flow shut around the drums and seal them, without any message, without any marker, without requiring a single future person to interpret a single symbol correctly. The medium is the message, and the message is *nothing here*, delivered in a language that predates life and will outlast it.

The markers above ground are for the interval before that happens — the awkward few centuries when the hole is still a hole and the danger is still reachable. They are a stopgap, and we have made them into a monument, because making monuments is what we do with things we cannot finish.

And still I think the attempt is worth something, even doomed. Not because it will work. Because *This place is not a place of honor* is one of the very few sentences our civilization has tried to write to people it will never meet, about a harm it will never see, with nothing to gain. There is no reciprocity available. The future cannot thank us, reward us, vote for us, or remember our names. We are spending real money and real ingenuity on strangers whose existence is a hypothesis. That is either the most absurd thing we do or very close to the best, and I genuinely cannot decide which, and I suspect the correct answer is that those are the same thing.

Somewhere out past the salt flats there may eventually be a field of concrete thorns, and someone will walk into it, and stop, and feel the hair rise on their arms, and not know why. If they turn around, we will have gotten through. Not the words — just the flinch. Maybe that's all that ever crosses.
